strings.text: A straw-tick pallet against the wall, blanket already turned down for whoever needs it.
Straw tick, borrowed blanket — Riverfarm always finds room for one more.
A ledger left open on the corner table, the same one he carries everywhere else. Columns re-summed in three different inks — he never trusts the first count, or the second.
Grain against debts, and the debts keep winning most years. Best not to read it over his shoulder.
A thin man with a hazel stick in each hand, laying them side by side against the light.
Sacks stacked low and a season coming for them. Lifting them above the flood line is work, and work is a Skill you either have or you don't.
Grain sacks stacked at ankle height on a shed floor, with the river three weeks out.
[Basic Cleaning] — You clear the shed floor and stack every sack up off the boards. The count comes right the moment anyone can see all of it at once.
[Basic Cooking] — You feed the flood crew out of the mill's own pot, and they work the shed twice over for it. The count comes right in the doing.
Something has been at the sacks in that corner. Nobody here has called it a problem yet, and it is not your count to go digging in.
Chaff scattered wide, sacks opened low down, and something breathing behind the last row.
A ladder down into a pit of black water, with the wheel standing still in it and the sluice pinned shut against the season.
The pinned sluice carries three seasons of high-water scratches, and each one sits higher than the last.
A shelf set higher on the wall than any shelf needs to be, with notches and years cut into the post beside it.
Somebody has cut a notch for every flood since before the village had a headman, and built the shelf a hand above the worst of them.
A bundle of split hazel sticks hung on a nail, each notched down one edge.
Split tallies. One half stays with the mill, one half goes home with the household, and neither can be altered alone.
Fresh-turned earth, packed and raised into a long low wall. Someone's been digging with purpose, not just drainage.
Just raised earth. Whatever it's for, nobody's finished it yet.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Rails re-set forty paces east of where they stood. The gap they left is the corusdeer road, and the hoof marks say the herd found it.
Rails re-set forty paces east of where they stood. The gap they left is the corusdeer road, and the hoof marks say the herd found it.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
Not now. Got a village to hold together.
A ledger under one arm, mud to the knee, the look of a man doing three jobs badly instead of one job well.
Ordinary, except for how still they stand, and a faint red thread at the wrist that doesn't match anything else they're wearing.
One long thatch ridge, twice the width of any cottage. Smoke curls from a vent at the peak even in daylight.
Hollow's not safe alone.
Rope-burned hands, a game bag, and wolf sign on his boots. Whatever he hunts, it walks on four legs.

A worn marker stone at the village's heart. Someone scratched a spiral into its face, long since softened by weather. Attunement is what markers like this are cut for: a door shown the right stone learns the place, and can open onto it ever after.
Cold, plain stone, and it stays cold for you. Whatever hung a door somewhere else hasn't hung one yet.
A narrow break in the treeline, west of the fields. The light changes past the first few trees.
Nothing there. Whatever you saw is gone with the light.
Eyes catch the light at the field's edge, gone again when you look straight at them. Only after dark.
Vines thicker than they should be, over the fence line and into the village since the thicket business settled. They creep across open ground, twitching against a wind that isn't blowing.
A plank of hooks at the fence line, each hook holding a scrap with a task on it and no name. Ditching, thatch, a fence a cow disagrees with. The scraps come down about as fast as they go up.
Every hook is bare. Riverfarm doesn't invent work to keep a stranger busy.
You take a scrap off its hook and spend the morning behind it. Ditching, mostly. The village pays coin because coin is the thing it has least of, and it pays on the day.
Somebody chalked your name against a hook before you got there. That is the whole of Riverfarm's vocabulary for gratitude, and it is not a small word.
The hook you get is the one nobody else will touch: the wet corner down by the river, every time. They give it to you because you finish it.
The mill's ground-floor door, set into the base of the tower on the river side. The sluice hums even with the wheel pinned.
Hurdle fencing the hunter threw up after the thicket business. Two ewe lambs inside it, and a third that will not put weight on a foreleg.
[Beast's Mending] — You strap the lamb's leg, and it stands on it before you have finished. The ewes crowd in to look.
The lambs have had their handling for today. Crowd them now and you undo it.
You get a hand under the limping one and hold it until it stops shaking. Fleece comes away on your fingers.
They come to the rail for you now. You work burrs out of three fleeces and leave the bad leg for last.
A scatter of old bones in the field grass, half sunk. The wolf keeps returning to it, head down, digging and stopping and digging again.
Under a stone, under the turf: a thin copper ring, polished bright by somebody's worried thumbs before they lost it here.
Turned earth, filled in and gone quiet. The wolf walks past it now.
The stringers are sound and the boards are somewhere downriver. Standing here wishing at it will not deck it.
Two stringers still run out along the bank from the cottage corner, and the decking between them is gone — lifted by a flood and never replaced. The beams are sound. It is boards it wants.
[Basic Repair] — You cut and lay boards across the stringers until the walk is a walk again. It holds when you lean on it, and it will hold tomorrow.
Clay-daub walls, a low thatch roof. A washing line strung between two posts.
Someone's home. Best not to just walk in.
The bank is cut clean through here, down to brown water. You could go the long way round the cottage, or somebody could put boards back across it.
Where the decking used to be there is a scoured trench down to the water, wider than a stride and undercut on both lips.
You get one sack up and your back tells you about the other eleven. This is a job for somebody built for it.
Grain sacks stacked off a dray at the bank head, waiting on however many trips it takes. Two men are looking at them the way you look at a long afternoon.
[Broader Shoulders] — You take three at once and walk them up to the shed without stopping. The dray is clear before the second man has picked up his first, and two coins come your way for it.
The dray is empty and the shed is full. Nothing more to shift today.
Dragging them one at a time will take all day. Carrying them properly would not.
A second cottage, smaller, its thatch newer than its neighbor's.
Someone's home. Best not to just walk in.
Sails turning slow in whatever wind there is. The grinding floor above the wheat fields.
The sails creak overhead. No one's tending it right now.
A stone-ringed well, rope worn smooth by years of hauling. The water's clean this far from the blight talk.
Cool water, a long way down. You leave the rope where you found it.
Bundled and stacked before the rain, the way a good harvest gets stored.
Straw and an old coat, arms out over the tilled rows. It isn't working today — there are crows on its own hat.
A plank pier reaching out over the river. The village's whole trade with anywhere downstream starts here (wiki Riverfarm, ch. 3.00-3.01 E: 'farming land fed by a river').
Weathered planks, sound underfoot. The current runs steady past the end of it.
Low fence rail, bordering the tilled rows.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A stone taller than it should be able to stand on its own, glowing faint purple at the seams.
Another of the ring-stones, humming faintly if you hold still.
Another of the ring-stones, humming faintly if you hold still.
Something's meant to go in this, cooked properly. You don't know your way around a stew pot. Yet.
An iron pot set by the cottage door, empty and waiting. Someone means for it to be used.
[Basic Cooking] — You cook the offering plain and honest, the way you'd feed anyone who'd walked far to eat.
The pot waits for something cooked plain and honest.
The kettle wants yarrow before it gives anything back.
A witch's cauldron, warm and waiting. Whatever it wants from you, it isn't just stirring.
[Hedge Remedy] — You stir like you're sorry for the sick, the way she said. What comes off the ladle is the color of meaning it.
The cauldron's lit and the water's talking to itself. Hands that mean it could bring a remedy out of that.
A row of cold candle-stubs, set either side of the door. Whatever lights them, it isn't a match.
Cold wax and old wicks, set along the threshold like they're waiting for something specific.
[Light] — The candles catch, one after another, without a flame ever touching them.
Cold candle-stubs either side of the door. No match will do it.
Roots and briar, knotted tighter than any plant ties itself. Whatever it's holding, an untrained eye won't find it.
A snarl of root and briar at the center of the standing stones, tied in a knot that doesn't look like it grew that way.

[Observe] — The knot isn't wood at all, once you look right at it: a price, tied off and waiting to be paid. You pay it yourself, plainly, and the tension goes out of the air like a held breath let go.
The knot is too deliberate for briar. It wants a closer look than eyes give for free.
A standing stone, older than the village and not saying anything about it.
[Detect Magic] — Light runs under the turf in one long seam, straight through the stone and away west. The hollow is built on a current.
The stone sits where the ground feels heaviest. That's not an accident.
Tea's still hot. The offer doesn't get warmer with asking twice.
A small grey witch in a hat pressed with tea leaves and old flowers. She holds a cup like the answer to a question you haven't asked yet.
Briars, moving without wind. They haven't noticed you yet.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
More briars, thicker here, coiled tight around something you can't quite see.
The trees thin out this way. Open fields past the last few trunks.
The brambles here twist into a tight loop, low to the ground. It doesn't look natural. You can't tell how to clear it without setting it off.
You work the knot loose one bramble at a time, careful of the thorns. Snagged in the weave: a coin, tarnished green from the damp.
The briar holds nothing new today.
Brambles knotted into a tight loop, low against the undergrowth. Nothing grows that way on its own.
A second, smaller house at the hollow's west edge, its roof half fallen in. The lintel is cut with a line of shallow marks, worn nearly smooth, and the door stands open on the dark.
The bracken is pressed flat and the smell of it is old. Nothing about this is your business until somebody tells you otherwise.
Bracken pressed flat in a hollow under the northern trees, and the smell of something that has been eating well.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A tree grown crooked, leaning in over the path like it's listening.
A mossy, sagging roof, a crooked chimney, and one window that's always lit no matter the hour.
The door's shut. Whatever's inside isn't asking for company right now.
A palm-sized shard of grey stone on the shelf, cut along one edge with marks you cannot read.
A shard of grey stone on the shelf, set down carefully by someone who meant to come back for it.

[Detect Magic] — The shard is one link of a boundary that used to ring the whole thicket. It still pulls, faintly, along the exact line the deer refuse to cross. It was drawn to keep something in, and it has been failing at that for a very long time.
The scrap hums under the dust, and not the way dust hums.
A row of stoppered jars along the top shelf, their labels faded to a suggestion.
Every stopper is waxed and every jar is still full. Whoever kept this house left it ready and never came back for it.
A rack of bundled stems, dried long past any use.
Yarrow, mostly, and a great deal of it. Somebody kept this place stocked for a house they intended to come back to.
Cold ash banked neatly against the back of the hearth.
The ash is banked the way you bank a fire you mean to wake in the morning. It has been cold for years.
One shutter, latched, with daylight coming through the slats in bars.
Latched from the inside, and the hut was shut when you found it. You decide not to work that through any further today.
